pr_title: loop-util: enable LO_FLAGS_DIRECT_IO by default on loopback devices
pr_comments:
That this is the right thing to do is discussed here btw, by the kernel people:

https://lore.kernel.org/linux-block/20211018150550.GA29993@lst.de/

Also see the discussions on #21003

issue_context.title: homed direct-io for [at least] btrfs luks images
issue_context.body:
Mounting of home volumes is currently done without direct-io loopback support. Maybe there's a reason for this, but it's extremely slow on my btrfs on luks on btrfs on luks configuration.

Copying/moving from my homed $HOME to a folder outside of $HOME yields about 150-250MBps on an NVMe.

Using losetup to switch the loopback device for my home folder to direct-io yields much faster speeds - over 1GBps.

If there's a reason that mounting the image file is done the current way, could we at least have a settable option for each user [homectl] and system default so it doesn't have to be changed after mounting/login every time?
comments:
The main reason is that documentation on this is so sparse... Do you have any hints where this is documented further?

Would there be any reason *not* to enable this? i.e. why doesn't `losetup` default to it?

But maybe we can steal tweaks like this from here:

https://android.googlesource.com/platform/system/apex/+/refs/heads/master/apexd/apexd_loop.cpp

Note to self: that android apexd code forcible sets the IO elevator for block devices to "noop". Current development kernels default to that anyway, hence I figure we should not copy that part of what apexd doess.

apexd also does the following:

1. Set the IO elevator queue depth of loopback devices to 2x the one of the underlying device
2. It sets the read-ahead to 128, which however is the default anyway afaics.
3. Invokes BLKFLSBUF ioctl after LOOP_SET_STATUS64 to work around some kernel bug (which might have been fixed by now?)
4. Sets the block size of the loopback device to 4096K unconditionally

Yeah. I can't find any real documentation, either positive or negative, on the DIO mode. 

The default block size is 512B, so 4096 would be a big difference. I didn't even realize the BS was that small. The K must be a typo though. I can't set a block size that large [with losetup anyway]. Just 4096B.

I did try my homed volume with the larger block size and didn't really notice a difference, with or without DIO.

DIO on is a huge difference though.

> The default block size is 512B, so 4096 would be a big difference. I didn't even realize the BS was that small. The K must be a typo though. I can't set a block size that large [with losetup anyway]. Just 4096B.

Yeah, the K was a typo. 

So, as it appears current kernels (>= 5.4) will propagate the block size automaticlly correctly, anyway, and we thus don't have to do anything anymore. 

So this means elevator and block size are nowadays set automatically by the kernel. The readahead of 128 is the default anyway. Which thus only leaves the BLKFLSBUF thing, and the queue length.

Kernel guys said this btw:

https://lore.kernel.org/linux-block/20211018150550.GA29993@lst.de/

Hence I prepped a fix for this in #21044. PTAL.

The BLKFLSBUF thing I thinkw as fixed with this:

https://git.kernel.org/pub/scm/linux/kernel/git/axboe/linux-block.git/commit/?h=for-linus&id=5db470e229e22b7eda6e23b5566e532c96fb5bc3

i.e. kernel 5.0.

Given we officially support kernels all the way back to 3.13 I figure this might be something to use as well.
